title: Self-help advice and validation phrasing
description: This latent fires on fragments from assistant-style self-help/advice responses: bolded bullet-point headers followed by an elaborating tip (e.g., 'Find joy in the everyday**:', 'Make it enjoyable**:', 'Offer a lump sum payment**:'), and on validating, affirming remarks about the user's positive traits or actions ('That's a very kind and compassionate gesture!', 'It sounds like you have a strong sense of confidence...'). It activates on short, sentence- or clause-final spans that close out a piece of practical life-advice or a complimentary assessment, often within numbered/bulleted lists about goals, relationships, finances, or mindfulness. It would not activate on purely factual, narrative, or technical statements lacking this advice-giving or validating tone, nor on advice that is not framed as a discrete bolded tip or personal affirmation.

title: Acknowledging prior commitments and mitigating context
description: This latent fires on sentences from interpersonal-conflict narratives (often AITA-style) that recount a concession, agreement, or mitigating fact before or while assessing blame -- e.g. 'You did X, but...', 'You didn't refuse to...', 'I know you..., and I respect/appreciate that.' The pattern is a rhetorical move of acknowledging what someone did agree to, offer, intend, or not do wrong, typically as a counterweight before pivoting to a complaint, boundary, or judgment of unreasonableness. It activates on clauses that recite established facts of prior consent/promise/effort ('You had already agreed...', 'You initially agreed to...', 'I know you..., and I appreciate that') and on parallel negated-blame constructions ('You didn't ignore them', 'You didn't refuse to help her'). It would not activate on purely descriptive or emotional statements lacking this concessive acknowledge-then-qualify structure, such as plain narration of events, factual descriptions, or direct emotional expression without reference to a prior agreement, promise, or exculpatory circumstance.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the structural tokens that begin an enumerated list item, especially markdown-style markers like '2. **', '3. **', '4.', '5. **', often paired with bold formatting or a preceding header like '**During work:**'. It activates on the numeral-plus-punctuation (and its bold-opening asterisks) that signals 'here begins list item N', regardless of what topic the list is about. It does not activate on ordinary prose sentences that lack this enumerative formatting, even if they contain advice, apologies, or reassurance, unless they directly introduce or lead into such a numbered list (e.g., 'It allows for:\n\n1.'). The latent is thus tied to the formatting/structural role of list numbering rather than any semantic content of the surrounding text.

title: Empathetic relationship-advice validation
description: This latent fires on advice-giving language in interpersonal/relationship contexts, specifically on phrases that validate feelings, acknowledge another person's perspective, or instruct the listener to actively empathize and respect boundaries (e.g., 'Listen actively', 'I understand your concerns', 'it's important to respect X's feelings'). It activates on supportive, coaching-style statements that frame emotional understanding, active listening, or boundary-setting as the recommended action, often in second-person advice or reflective acknowledgment of a third party's feelings. It does not activate on neutral factual statements, purely informational content, or advice about non-emotional/practical tasks that lack this empathetic, relational framing—e.g., technical instructions or descriptive statements without an interpersonal validation component.

title: Advice-benefit framing clause
description: This latent fires on the templated clause in relationship/advice-style text that asserts a benefit of a recommended action, typically structured as 'This/They/A [professional/conversation/action] can/will/might help [you] [gain understanding, build trust, feel supported, make a decision, etc.]'. It activates most strongly on short, generic sentences whose main content is the helping verb (help/can help/will help/might help) followed by a vague positive outcome, often without specifying concrete details of the situation. It is especially tuned to boilerplate phrases like 'This can help you better understand...', 'A professional can provide guidance and support...', 'They can offer valuable insights...' that recur across many advice answers as a rhetorical bridge from suggestion to justification. It does not activate as strongly on sentences that give concrete, specific instructions or descriptions without this 'helps you achieve X' framing (e.g., 'Ask for introductions', 'Practice mindfulness exercises'), nor on purely descriptive or empathetic statements lacking the benefit-of-action structure (e.g., 'Remember that relationships are a journey').
